newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaraguan president closes door to new state jobs.
newsitem.headline: Nicaraguan president closes door to new state jobs.

text.p: Nicaraguan President Arnoldo Aleman, who has pledged to bring capitalist prosperity to his impoverished country, has made one thing clear in his first six weeks in office -- the state will no longer be Nicaragua's employer of last resort.

Aleman, the former right-wing mayor of Managua, took power on Jan. 10 promising to lower sky-high unemployment and set loose market forces in Nicaragua, which had a socialist government from 1979 to 1990 and suffered an economic meltdown during a civil war involving U.S.-backed Contra rebels.

He inherited a tiny economy that had grown for three consecutive years -- reaching 5.5 percent in 1996 -- following an economic collapse that saw annual per capita income fall from $1,122 in 1978 to $430 in 1990, according to Ministry of the Economy figures.
Riding a wave of economic optimism, he promised to create 100,000 jobs a year while reducing the size of Nicaragua's bloated public sector.
Brandishing a pair of scissors on Monday, Aleman cut up state credit cards once held by government ministers to launch a fiscal austerity programme that included a freeze on government hiring.
The message was clear: job growth would be come in the private sector and the days of the state as employer were gone.
"People should look for other ways to live and not through the enormous state apparatus that now has more than 82,000 employees," Aleman told a news conference.

But economists warned that even with high economic growth in 1997, the private sector would not generate enough jobs to lower Nicaragua's unemployment and meet the high expectations Aleman's government has created.

"I think the government of Aleman has climbed on a wave of economic growth that has been in the making for three years, and this wave will bring higher economic growth in 1997 than last year," Alejandro Martinez Cuenca, a former left-wing central banker and head of the International Foundation for the Global Economic Challege, told Reuters on Thursday.
"But the dilemma facing Aleman is that independent of this high economic growth, the work force is growing so rapidly that unemployment will not fall," he said.
According to a 1995 census, 45 percent of Nicaraguans were under 15 years of age and rapidly entering the work force.
Martinez said he calculated that Nicaragua would have more than one million unemployed or underemployed people by the end of 1997. It had 890,000 in 1996.
The government estimated that 52 percent of Nicaragua's workers were currently unemployed or underemployed.
By promising to create jobs and lower unemployment, Aleman has set himself up for a potential fall when down the road people find themslves unemployed, Martinez said.
"Everything that creates false expectations sooner or later comes back to haunt those in power and I think this is a risk he has assumed, announcing a certain number of jobs," he said.
